specPoints.text: know that the initial linear region of a force-extension graph is associated with Hooke’s law
describe elastic behaviour as the ability of a material to recover its original shape after the forces causing deformation have been removed

primer.text: Stretch something gently and it obeys; stretch it too far and it betrays you. Hooke's law is the obedience — extension proportional to force up to a limit — and elastic behaviour is the full recovery afterwards. This note draws the graph, names the limit, and sorts materials by their recovery.

lessons.title: Hooke's law and the force-extension graph
lessons.opening: Stretch something gently and it obeys; stretch it too far and it betrays you. Hooke's law is the obedience — extension tracking the applied force point-for-point until the limit of proportionality ends the agreement. This lesson draws the graph, names the limit, and shows where the straight region ends.
keyPoints: Hooke's law: an elastic object's extension answers point-for-point to the applied force, until the limit of proportionality.
Directly proportional means doubling the force doubles the extension, and halving the force halves it.
The limit of proportionality is the point beyond which force and extension are no longer proportional.
On a force-extension graph the law is the initial straight-line (linear) region.
The limit's position varies from material to material.

low.restatement: Double the pull, double the stretch — until the limit, where the deal ends.
low.analogy: A fair taxi meter: every extra newton buys the same extra stretch, until the meter's rules change at the limit.
low.examPointer: Quote the law with its escape clause — 'up to the limit of proportionality' — or the statement is incomplete.

medium.restatement: The graph's geometry is the law: the linear region's straightness is the proportionality, and the bend marks the limit; the limit is material-specific, not universal.
medium.analogy: A rubber ruler drawn on elastic: the printed centimetres obey while the elastic is fresh, then drift once it is overstretched.
medium.examPointer: Graph questions: identify the linear region, mark the limit, and state what changes there — three marks, three statements.

check.stem: Hooke's law says that stretching an elastic object gives an extension which is:

options.explanation: The proportionality is direct, not inverse.

options.text: Proportional to the applied force, but only as far as the limit of proportionality
options.explanation: The law of record, escape clause included.

options.text: Equal to the force in newtons
options.explanation: Extension is a length, not a force.
The whole law is the relationship.

check.stem: On a force-extension graph, Hooke's law corresponds to:

options.explanation: The curve is past the limit.
The area is not the law's home.
The law lives in the line's shape, not an axis.

check.stem: A spring stretches 4 cm under a 2 N load. Assuming Hooke's law holds, a 4 N load stretches it:

options.explanation: Doubling the force doubles the extension.
The extension must answer the doubled force.

check.stem: Beyond the limit of proportionality, the force-extension graph:

options.explanation: The graph does not rewind itself.

options.text: Curves away from the straight line
options.explanation: The proportionality fails and the line bends.

check.stem: 'Directly proportional' means that doubling the force:

check.modelAnswer: An elastic object's extension answers point-for-point to the force applied — double the pull, double the stretch — and the agreement holds only up to the limit of proportionality.

check.stem: What does the initial straight region of a force-extension graph indicate?
check.modelAnswer: That force and extension are proportional there — the linear region associated with Hooke's law.

check.stem: Explain why the graph bends beyond the limit of proportionality.
check.modelAnswer: Past the limit the material no longer follows the proportional rule: each extra newton no longer buys the same extra stretch. The plotted points therefore leave the straight line and curve.

check.stem: A spring stretches 4 cm under a 2 N load. What extension does a 6 N load produce, assuming the law still holds?
check.modelAnswer: Extension is proportional to force: 6 N is three times 2 N, so the extension is 3 × 4 = 12 cm.

lessons.title: Elastic behaviour and deformation
lessons.opening: Deformation is any change of an object's original shape, and it comes in two kinds: elastic, where the shape recovers once the forces let go, and inelastic, where the change is permanent. The unloaded spring springs back; the moulded clay keeps its new form.
keyPoints: Elastic behaviour: the material regains the shape it started with once the deforming forces are gone.
Deformation is a change in the object's original shape.
Elastic deformation is not permanent: the object returns to its original shape.
Inelastic deformation is permanent: the object keeps its new shape.
Rubber bands, fabrics and steel springs deform elastically; plastic, clay and glass deform inelastically.

low.restatement: Let go and the shape either comes back (elastic) or stays changed (inelastic).
low.analogy: A hotel bed: the mattress recovers by morning (elastic); the dent in the chocolate bar does not (inelastic).
low.examPointer: The definition of record centres on recovery after the forces are removed — quote it whole.

medium.restatement: The classification is about the material's response, not the force's size — though the same material can cross from elastic to inelastic behaviour past its limit.
medium.analogy: A paperclip bends gently and springs back, bent harder and it keeps the kink: same clip, two regimes.
medium.examPointer: Examples earn marks: springs, rubber bands and fabrics for elastic; plastic, clay and glass for inelastic.

check.stem: Elastic behaviour means the material can:

options.explanation: Deformation happens; the point is the recovery.

options.text: Recover the shape it started with once the deforming forces are gone
A change in the object's original shape
A loss of the object's mass
options.explanation: Mass is untouched by shape changes.

options.text: A rise in the object's temperature
A change of the object's colour
A rubber band snapping back after release
A steel spring returning to length

options.explanation: The kept shape is the inelastic signature.
Both are inelastic examples of record.
Both recover — the elastic examples of record.

check.stem: Moulding clay keeps its new form after the hands stop. The deformation is:

options.text: Inelastic — the shape change is permanent
Elastic — the clay will recover overnight

options.explanation: Every deformation is one of the two kinds.
The classification does not depend on a rescue process.

check.modelAnswer: It is the material's capacity to return to the shape it started with once the forces causing the deformation are taken away.

check.stem: Define deformation and name its two kinds.
check.modelAnswer: A change of the object's original shape; it is elastic when the shape recovers and inelastic when the change is permanent.

check.stem: Explain why a steel spring is classed as elastic while modelling clay is not.
check.modelAnswer: The unloaded spring returns to its starting length, so its shape change was not permanent — elastic behaviour. Clay keeps the moulded form after the hands stop, a permanent change, so it is inelastic.

check.stem: A spring is stretched 5 cm; the load is removed but the spring stays 5 cm longer. Classify the deformation and name a material that would have recovered.
check.modelAnswer: The 5 cm remains, so the deformation is inelastic; a rubber band — or a fresh steel spring within its limit — would have recovered its original shape.

glossary.definition: The law that extension is directly proportional to applied force, up to the limit of proportionality.
The point beyond which force and extension stop being proportional.
Recovering the original shape once the deforming forces are removed.
A permanent shape change: the object does not recover after the forces are removed.
